>ポイント</div>\n <p>慣性系から見て、物体は $y$ 軸上の $y:
>Key points

In the inertial frame, the object moves in uniform straight-line motion along the $y$ axis starting from $y=y_0$ with velocity $v$. $v>0$ is away from the origin; $v<0$ is toward the origin. When approaching, it passes through the origin and continues to the opposite side. No forces act. We view this from a coordinate frame rotating with angular velocity $\omega$. On a wide screen the layouts are side by side; on a narrow screen they are stacked. Top or left is the ground frame; bottom or right is the person's frame.

Since the true force is $\vec{0}$, the equations of motion in the rotating frame are

$$\begin{cases}\tilde{x}''(t)=2\omega\tilde{y}'(t)+\omega^{2}\tilde{x}(t)\\ \tilde{y}''(t)=-2\omega\tilde{x}'(t)+\omega^{2}\tilde{y}(t)\end{cases}$$

When the axes of the two frames coincide at $t=0$, the solution is

$$\tilde{x}(t)=(y_0+vt)\sin\omega t,\quad \tilde{y}(t)=(y_0+vt)\cos\omega t$$

The distance from the origin is $r=\lvert y_0+vt\rvert$. While $y_0=0$ and $v>0$, using the angle $\theta=\omega t$ measured from the rotating frame's $y$ axis gives

$$r=\frac{v}{\omega}\theta$$

After passing the origin, the spiral shrinks once and then expands again on the opposite side. The velocity that enters the Coriolis force is the velocity as seen in this rotating frame, and its direction is to the right of the direction of motion.
>ポイント</div>\n <p>水平な床の上で、物体は止まっています。働く力:
>Key points

On a horizontal floor, the object is at rest. No forces act. A person at the center looks at this object while rotating with angular velocity $\omega$. On a wide screen the layouts are side by side; on a narrow screen they are stacked. Top or left is the ground frame; bottom or right is the person's frame. This is the special case of uniform straight-line motion with $v=0$, and the distance from the center is $R=\lvert y_0\rvert$.

From the person's view, the object moves on a circle of radius $R$ at speed $\omega R$. The centripetal force required for this apparent circular motion is the inward

$$m\frac{(\omega R)^{2}}{R}=m\omega^{2}R$$

In the person's frame, an outward centrifugal force $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}R$ and an inward Coriolis force $\displaystyle 2m\omega^{2}R$ act. Taking outward as positive,

$$F_{\mathrm{cen}}=m\omega^{2}R,\quad F_{\mathrm{Cor}}=-2m\omega^{2}R$$

The net force is the inward $\displaystyle m\omega^{2}R$, matching the apparent centripetal force. The velocity that enters the Coriolis force is the velocity as seen in this rotating frame. The floor pattern is fixed to the ground, so it appears to rotate opposite to the object.
